cues.text: Welcome to Organic Nitrogen.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Classify an amine by counting carbon groups directly bonded to nitrogen.
One carbon group gives a primary amine, two give a secondary amine and three
give a tertiary amine.
Branching elsewhere in the carbon skeleton does not change that count.
Thus tert butylamine is primary even though the carbon attached to nitrogen
has
three carbon neighbours.
Dimethylamine is secondary and trimethylamine is tertiary.
A quaternary ammonium ion has four carbon groups on nitrogen and a positive
charge; it is a different class from a neutral tertiary amine.
In aniline, nitrogen is directly attached to a benzene ring, allowing its lone
pair to conjugate with the ring.
In benzylamine, a saturated carbon separates nitrogen from the ring.
That difference affects basicity and reactivity.
An amide instead has nitrogen directly attached to a carbonyl carbon.
Delocalization into the carbonyl strongly reduces the nitrogen lone pair's
availability compared with an ordinary amine.
Draw nitrogen's immediate neighbours before classifying a structure.
An amine's nitrogen lone pair can accept a proton to form an ammonium ion.
Basicity measures the equilibrium tendency for that proton transfer in a
specified solvent.
A larger base equilibrium constant means a stronger base under comparable
conditions.
The conjugate acid and base constants are related through the water ion
product.
At twenty five degrees Celsius, take that product as ten raised to the power
minus fourteen.
If the conjugate acid has an acid constant of ten to the minus ten, dividing
the water ion product by it gives a base constant of ten to the minus four.
The corresponding acid and base logarithmic values are ten and four, adding to
fourteen.
An acid logarithmic value of five instead gives a base logarithmic value of
nine, indicating a weaker base.
Always identify whether the supplied value describes the amine or its
conjugate
acid.
Structural effects help explain the comparison: alkyl groups can donate
electron density, while aniline's nitrogen lone pair participates in aromatic
conjugation.
Electron withdrawing substituents, steric crowding and solvent stabilization
can all affect the observed equilibrium.
Alkyl groups can donate electron density, suggesting increased intrinsic
proton
affinity as substitution increases.
In water, however, the neutral amine and its conjugate acid are solvated
differently.
Hydrogen bonding, steric crowding and solvation of the charged product can
change the ordering.
A universal tertiary > secondary > primary rule in aqueous solution is
unreliable.
If a problem supplies K b or conjugate acid p K a values measured under
comparable conditions, use those data rather than a memorized slogan.
For example, a conjugate acid with p K a 10 corresponds to a stronger base
than
one with p K a 5 in the same solvent and convention.
These numbers are illustrative, not values assigned to unspecified real
compounds.
For illustrative bases A and B with conjugate acid p K a values ten and five,
their acid constants differ by one hundred thousand.
Their base constants differ by the inverse factor, making A the stronger base
by that equilibrium measure.
This is a ratio of constants under comparable conditions, not a statement that
every solution has a one hundred thousand fold difference in p H or reaction
rate.
Preparation of an amine must be checked by following every carbon atom.
A nitrile contains a carbon bonded to nitrogen through a triple bond.
Suitable reduction converts that nitrile carbon into the carbon of a methylene
group attached to amino nitrogen.
Acetonitrile starts with two carbons and gives ethylamine, which still has
two.
Reduction of an aromatic nitro group can give aniline without changing the
ring's carbon framework.
A different preparation, Hofmann rearrangement of a primary amide, shortens
the
carbon chain of the organic amine by one.
Acetamide has two carbons but gives methylamine with one carbon because its
carbonyl carbon leaves the selected organic product.
That carbon remains accounted for elsewhere in the overall reaction.
Ammonia reacting with a suitable alkyl halide can form an amine, but further
alkylation may produce mixtures.
Gabriel synthesis is another route for suitable primary alkyl substrates and
does not imply ordinary substitution on an unactivated aryl halide.
Identify the starting functional group, select appropriate conditions and
compare the carbon counts before naming the final amine.
The carbylamine test is associated with primary aliphatic and aromatic amines;
secondary and tertiary amines do not give that same reaction.
It produces an isocyanide under the specified test conditions.
In the Hinsberg distinction, primary and secondary amines can form different
sulfonamide products, while tertiary amines do not form the same nitrogen
hydrogen derived product.
A primary amine sulfonamide retains an acidic nitrogen hydrogen and can
dissolve in alkali; the secondary amine product lacks that hydrogen and is not
similarly alkali soluble.
Check the subsequent acid/base behaviour rather than relying only on a
precipitate.
The primary amine starting material has two nitrogen hydrogen bonds; its
sulfonamide product retains one.
A secondary amine begins with one such hydrogen and loses it during
sulfonamide
formation, leaving no nitrogen hydrogen in that product.
This explains the different alkaline behaviour more precisely than saying
primary amines dissolve and secondary amines never dissolve.
Solubility also depends on protonation, solvent and the exact compound.
Aniline reacts with nitrous acid generated under cold acidic conditions to
form
a benzenediazonium salt.
The usual elementary temperature window is about two hundred seventy three to
two hundred seventy eight kelvin.
Aromatic diazonium salts are useful intermediates in cold solution; they
should
not be described as indefinitely stable or safe to isolate dry.
A primary aliphatic amine can form a much less stable aliphatic diazonium
species that loses nitrogen and leads to further products.
Secondary amines instead can form N nitrosamines under appropriate nitrosating
conditions; they do not follow the same primary aromatic diazotization
sequence.
Always identify the original nitrogen class and the aromatic attachment before
choosing the pathway.
Cold aromatic diazonium formation and later warming are separate stages with
different purposes.
In a conceptual aniline to phenol sequence, first create the diazonium group
under suitable cold acidic conditions, then replace it during aqueous warming.
The six ring carbons remain throughout.
Different classes of amines react differently with nitrous acid, so the
reagent
name alone cannot establish that a diazonium salt is the final product.
A benzenediazonium group can be replaced by chloride or bromide using suitable
copper halide with copper in oxidation state plus one conditions, or by
cyanide
using the corresponding copper reagent in a Sandmeyer transformation.
Iodide substitution and other replacement routes use different conditions.
Write the reagent explicitly instead of treating every replacement as the same
copper catalysed process.
Warming a suitable aqueous diazonium solution can give phenol with nitrogen
loss.
Introducing CN adds a carbon to the organic product; replacing the group with
hydroxyl or Cl does not.
Diazonium chemistry therefore connects amines with aromatic compounds that are
difficult to obtain by simple direct substitution of an ordinary aryl halide.
Replacing the diazonium group of a six carbon ring by chlorine preserves six
carbons.
Replacing it by a cyano group gives a seven carbon nitrile because the new
group contains carbon.
Nitrogen gas loss occurs in either replacement, yet the final organic nitrogen
content differs: the cyano product still contains a nitrogen atom from the
introduced reagent.
Track each group's source rather than counting only the starting nitrogen.
A diazonium species can act as an electrophile towards an activated aromatic
ring, producing an azo linkage joining two aromatic groups.
Phenol is commonly coupled under suitably alkaline conditions and aniline
under
controlled mildly acidic conditions.
The medium matters because it controls ring activation and the form of the
reacting groups.
Coupling often favours the para site when it is available; an occupied para
position can change the outcome.
Conjugated azo products can be strongly coloured, but not every colour or
shade
is predictable from a reaction label alone.
For synthesis questions, track whether nitrogen is retained as an azo bridge
or
lost as nitrogen gas during replacement.
Azo coupling joins two aromatic partners through a nitrogen nitrogen double
bond.
If each partner is a six carbon ring without carbon side chains, the product
contains twelve carbons and the azo bridge contributes no carbon.
Replacement of a diazonium group by hydroxyl instead keeps only the original
ring in that product.
These different outcomes explain why coupling and replacement cannot be
treated
as interchangeable arrows in a synthesis plan.
Amine preparation routes can give different carbon skeletons even when all
products are primary amines.
Reduction of propanenitrile retains its nitrile carbon, producing the three
carbon primary amine propylamine.
In contrast, Hofmann rearrangement of propanamide produces ethylamine, with
one
fewer carbon than the starting amide.
The amide carbonyl carbon does not remain in that amine skeleton.
Gabriel synthesis provides another planning route: a suitable primary alkyl
halide is converted through a phthalimide intermediate and then released as a
primary amine.
Bromoethane can therefore lead to ethylamine without adding a carbon to its
ethyl group.
Ordinary Gabriel alkylation is not a general preparation of aniline from an
aryl halide, because the required substitution chemistry is different.
Do not confuse the names Hofmann rearrangement and Hofmann elimination; they
describe different transformations.
Write the carbon count beside both starting material and proposed product
before choosing a named reaction.
The route must fit the substrate as well as the desired nitrogen substitution
class.
Acylation attaches an acyl group to a nitrogen nucleophile and changes its
electronic properties.
A primary or secondary amine with a nitrogen hydrogen can form an amide with a
suitable acylating reagent.
A tertiary amine has no nitrogen hydrogen and does not give the same ordinary
neutral amide by this substitution.
It may still participate in other reactions or act as a base, so the absence
of
that product is not universal inertness.
Aniline can be converted into acetanilide by introducing an acetyl group on
nitrogen.
The nitrogen lone pair then interacts with the carbonyl, reducing its
availability and moderating the strong activation associated with free amino
substitution on the ring.
This is useful in reaction planning where the amino group must be protected or
its reactivity controlled.
Subsequent suitable hydrolysis can restore the amine.
Acylation is distinct from alkylation: the new group contains a carbonyl and
the product is an amide.
Track the atom receiving the group instead of assuming every new carbon group
on nitrogen produces another simple amine.
The Hinsberg comparison distinguishes amine classes through reaction and
solubility evidence rather than by counting alkyl groups in a name alone.
In the standard model, a primary amine forms a sulfonamide that retains a
nitrogen hydrogen.
That hydrogen can be removed by alkali, giving a soluble ionic form under the
stated conditions.
Acidification can return the neutral sulfonamide.
A secondary amine forms a sulfonamide without that nitrogen hydrogen, so it
lacks the same alkali dissolution step in the introductory comparison.
A tertiary amine does not form the corresponding sulfonamide in this test but
can dissolve in dilute acid by forming an ammonium salt.
Distinguish absence of a derivative from inability to form any salt.
The observations depend on the specified substrate and medium, and solubility
on its own is not a complete structure identification.
Draw the nitrogen substituents in the proposed derivative before selecting the
class.
This reasoning concerns interpretation of a supplied test sequence, not a
procedure for handling the reagent in a laboratory.
An aromatic diazonium group is a useful junction for several replacement
reactions.
In the usual aniline preparation, nitrous acid is generated under cold acidic
conditions and the diazonium salt is handled as a condition dependent
intermediate.
Different reagents then lead to different ring substituents.
Copper one chloride or bromide supports the corresponding halogen replacement
in the familiar Sandmeyer pattern.
Copper one cyanide introduces a nitrile group, while suitable warm aqueous
conditions can lead to phenol with nitrogen release.
Count carbons when the incoming group contains carbon.
Starting from a six carbon aniline ring, replacement by hydroxyl gives a six
carbon phenol, but replacement by cyanide gives seven carbon benzonitrile.
Hydrolysis of that nitrile can then give seven carbon benzoic acid.
The nitrogen atoms in the departing diazonium group do not become the nitrile
nitrogen by simple retention; identify the incoming reagent.
Reaction maps should label both the replacing group and the conditions, rather
than drawing one unspecified arrow that could mean several incompatible
products.
Base strength comparisons become quantitative when the constants refer to the
same solvent and temperature.
A smaller p K b means a larger base dissociation constant.
For illustrative bases with p K b values four and nine in water at twenty five
degrees Celsius, their base constants are ten to the minus four and ten to the
minus nine.
The first is one hundred thousand times larger.
This ratio does not mean the hydroxide concentrations must have the same ratio
in arbitrary solutions, because concentration and equilibrium balances still
matter.
For a conjugate acid and base pair in water, their constants multiply to the
water ion product.
At this temperature, p K a of the conjugate acid plus p K b of the base is
approximately fourteen.
Thus a base with p K b four has conjugate acid p K a about ten.
At a different temperature, use the appropriate water constant.
Do not combine a gas phase basicity ranking with aqueous constants or assume
that electron donation, resonance and solvation always produce the same amine
ordering.
The Gabriel synthesis is a reaction planning tool for a suitable primary
alkylamine, rather than a promise that every halide gives any desired amine.
In the elementary scheme, a phthalimide nitrogen nucleophile displaces halide
from a suitable alkyl carbon.
Subsequent cleavage of the protecting imide framework releases the primary
amine.
With a two carbon alkyl fragment, the resulting amine contains that same two
carbon fragment attached to nitrogen.
The imide ring is a temporary carrier; its carbons are not all incorporated
into the target alkylamine.
Ordinary unactivated chlorobenzene does not undergo the same backside
displacement at its aromatic carbon, so this simple route is not a general
preparation of aniline from chlorobenzene.
Tertiary alkyl substrates also do not become good ordinary backside
substitution partners merely because the named reaction is requested.
The method avoids describing an uncontrolled sequence of repeated alkylations
as a selective preparation of one primary amine.
Identify the reacting carbon, its substitution pattern, and the nitrogen
containing fragment that remains after release.
These are connectivity predictions for the stated model, not experimental
handling instructions or a claim that every substrate gives quantitative
conversion.
Gas evolution from a nitrogen reaction must be interpreted with the substrate
class and the gas collection model stated.
A simple primary aliphatic amine can react through an unstable aliphatic
diazonium intermediate that loses nitrogen gas.
In the elementary quantitative model, each mole of reacting primary amine
gives
one mole of nitrogen molecules, although the organic product distribution need
not be uniquely predicted for every substrate.
Suppose a supplied experiment reports twenty four point zero millilitres of
dry
nitrogen at three hundred kelvin and one hundred kilopascals, with ideal gas
behaviour and quantitative collection.
Use R equal to eight point three one four litre kilopascals per mole kelvin.
The nitrogen amount is about zero point zero zero zero nine six two mole.
That is also the reacting amine amount under the one to one model.
A twenty five point zero millilitre aliquot would therefore contain about zero
point zero three eight five molar reactive primary amine.
Wet gas would need a water vapour correction.
A primary aromatic amine can instead form an arenediazonium salt under the
specified diazotization conditions; do not automatically apply the same
immediate gas assay to every nitrogen compound.
The presence of a nitrogen atom does not make every nitrogen compound equally
basic.
In a simple alkylamine, the nitrogen lone pair can accept a proton, with
measured basicity also depending on solvent and other structural effects.
In an amide, that lone pair interacts with the adjacent carbonyl system.
Resonance descriptions include a contribution with positive charge on nitrogen
and negative charge on oxygen, while the real molecule is not switching
between
isolated drawings.
The carbon nitrogen bond consequently has partial double bond character, and
the nitrogen lone pair is less freely available than in the corresponding
simple amine.
Under ordinary strongly acidic protonation discussions, amides commonly
protonate preferentially on oxygen rather than behaving exactly like an
alkylamine at nitrogen.
This explains why converting an amine into an amide changes its basicity and
is
useful in protection strategies.
It does not mean every amide is completely unable to interact with acid or
that
a resonance drawing supplies a numerical base constant.
Compare actual structures and matching solvent data.
An amine classification based on carbon groups directly bonded to nitrogen
also
should not silently replace the distinct functional group identification of an
amide.
A nitrogen atom ledger distinguishes diazonium replacement from azo coupling.
In the elementary diazotization accounting, one nitrogen comes from the
original primary aromatic amino group and another from the nitrosating source.
The arenediazonium group therefore contains two nitrogen atoms attached as a
single group to the aromatic framework.
In a replacement reaction that releases nitrogen gas, both atoms leave that
organic framework together as one nitrogen molecule.
The incoming replacement group can have its own atoms, so product composition
must still be counted separately.
In azo coupling with an appropriate activated aromatic partner, the nitrogen
nitrogen unit is retained between the two aromatic fragments instead.
A benzene derived diazonium fragment has six carbons; a phenol partner
contributes another six.
The simple hydroxyazobenzene connectivity contains twelve carbons and two azo
nitrogens.
If an isotope marks one of the nitrogen sources in the ideal accounting model,
replacement sends that marked atom into the released nitrogen, while coupling
retains it in the azo unit.
This ledger does not specify every isotope exchange pathway, the coupling
position under every condition, or an experimental isolation procedure.
Use it to distinguish which bond connection and which atom inventory are
actually being tested.
The carbylamine reaction is useful as a structural identification principle
for
primary amines.
In its familiar net equation, one primary amine combines with one chloroform
and three potassium hydroxide units to form an isocyanide, three potassium
chloride units and three water molecules.
Both primary aliphatic and primary aromatic amines can fit this standard test.
Ordinary secondary and tertiary amines do not give the corresponding positive
test.
The product connectivity matters: an isocyanide has the organic group bonded
to
nitrogen, followed by the terminal carbon.
A nitrile instead has the organic group bonded directly to the nitrile carbon.
Starting with ethylamine, the two carbon ethyl group remains attached to
nitrogen, while chloroform supplies a third carbon to the isocyanide group.
This does not extend the ethyl carbon chain into a propyl group.
In a stipulated complete net conversion of zero point zero one zero zero mole
primary amine, the theoretical isocyanide amount is the same and the hydroxide
amount is three times as large.
This equation is an atom ledger and identification concept, not an instruction
to perform or smell a hazardous test.
An amine alkylation question must distinguish a desired substitution from
further reaction of the product.
Consider a stipulated sequence of successive methylations beginning with
methylamine.
The first added methyl group gives dimethylamine, and a second gives
trimethylamine.
These steps replace nitrogen hydrogen bonds with nitrogen carbon bonds after
the necessary proton transfer.
A third added methyl group gives tetramethylammonium, which can be present as
its iodide salt when methyl iodide supplies the groups.
Count the carbons: the starting amine contains one methyl carbon and the final
cation contains four.
Count nitrogen bonds separately.
Trimethylamine has three carbon bonds and a lone pair, whereas the quaternary
ammonium ion has four carbon bonds and a positive formal charge.
It is not normally classified as a fourth degree amine with an available lone
pair for ordinary amine protonation.
In actual alkylation, product mixtures and repeated alkylation can make
selective preparation difficult.
The arrow sequence therefore describes possible successive transformations,
not
a promise that each reagent addition yields one pure intermediate.
Track added groups, nitrogen hydrogen bonds and charge at every stage.
The basicity of an amine also determines how much is neutral at a specified
solution pH.
Write the conjugate acid equilibrium as protonated base giving neutral base
and
a proton.
In the ideal concentration approximation, the ratio of protonated to neutral
base equals ten raised to the conjugate acid p K a minus the p H.
Suppose the supplied conjugate acid p K a is nine and an external system
maintains p H seven.
The ratio is one hundred to one, so the neutral fraction is one divided by one
hundred and one, approximately zero point nine nine percent.
The protonated fraction is approximately ninety nine point zero one percent.
At maintained p H eleven the ratio reverses to one to one hundred, and the
neutral fraction becomes approximately ninety nine point zero one percent.
These calculations use the stated p H; they do not determine the p H of an
isolated weak base solution from its analytical concentration.
Acidic aqueous conditions can therefore favour an ammonium salt, while
increased p H can increase the neutral amine fraction.
Partition into another phase would need additional equilibrium information.
The amino group strongly activates an aromatic ring toward electrophilic
substitution.
In the familiar bromine water comparison, aniline can give two four six
tribromoaniline rather than stopping at one bromine substituent.
A protection strategy changes that behaviour.
Acylating the amino group gives acetanilide, whose nitrogen lone pair is also
involved with the carbonyl group.
Under suitable controlled bromination conditions, the protected ring gives
mainly the para brominated product.
Hydrolysis of the protecting group then gives para bromoaniline.
The para preference is a usual major product description, not a universal
claim
of complete selectivity under every condition.
Follow the temporary carbon inventory as well as the bromine count.
Aniline begins with six carbons, acetyl protection adds two, and bromination
leaves all eight carbons in the protected molecule.
Removal of the acetyl group returns the target amine to six carbons.
Direct tribromination installs three bromines, whereas the protected
monobromination route targets one.
A protecting group therefore changes reactivity temporarily and is later
removed; it is not an extra carbon fragment retained in the intended final
aromatic amine.
Reducing a nitro group to an amine retains the nitrogen and carbon skeleton
but
changes the nitrogen oxidation state.
For a nitro group bonded to carbon, nitrogen is formally plus three; in the
corresponding primary amine it is minus three.
The change therefore requires six electrons per nitrogen.
A balanced acidic half reaction can be written with one nitro compound, six
hydrogen ions and six electrons forming the neutral amine and two waters.
If the specified product is the protonated amine in an acidic mixture, add one
more hydrogen ion and write an ammonium product instead.
That extra proton is acid base bookkeeping, not a seventh reduction electron.
Thus an ideal zero point zero one zero zero mole nitrobenzene conversion needs
zero point zero six zero zero mole electrons for aniline formation.
Actual reagent demand also depends on competing reactions and the oxidation
product of the reducing agent.
Do not replace the nitro nitrogen with nitrogen from the acid or assume that
it
leaves as nitrogen gas.
This reduction is different from diazonium replacement and from an amide
rearrangement that changes carbon count.
Two reactions named Hofmann must not be confused.
The amide rearrangement makes an amine with one fewer carbon in its skeleton.
Hofmann elimination instead concerns a suitable quaternary ammonium species
and
can produce an alkene plus a tertiary amine.
In a supporting ethyltrimethylammonium hydroxide model, the ethyl group
supplies a beta hydrogen.
Elimination gives ethene, trimethylamine and water.
Count five carbons initially: two in the ethyl group and three in methyl
groups.
The products divide them into two carbons in ethene and three in
trimethylamine; no carbon has vanished as a carboxyl derivative.
The carbon bearing nitrogen is alpha, and the adjacent ethyl carbon bearing
the
eliminated hydrogen is beta.
A tetramethylammonium ion has no such beta carbon and cannot follow this
ordinary alkene forming beta elimination.
Where alternative beta sites exist, the familiar Hofmann comparison often
favours a less substituted alkene, but substrate geometry and the stated
conditions still matter.
This supporting distinction is not a general claim that heating any amine
releases an alkene or that every named Hofmann process has the same carbon
ledger.
An aromatic directing argument must use the species present in the reaction
medium.
Neutral aniline has a nitrogen lone pair that can donate toward the ring,
favouring ortho and para electrophilic substitution.
In a strongly acidic nitration mixture, much of it is converted into
anilinium.
That nitrogen bears a positive charge and no available lone pair for the same
donation, so the anilinium substituent is deactivating and meta directing.
Direct nitration is therefore not accurately summarized as clean para
substitution of unchanged neutral aniline.
Mixtures and other complications can occur; a large meta contribution does not
establish a universal pure meta product.
Protecting the amino group as an amide before the stated nitration changes
basicity and moderates activation, and suitable subsequent hydrolysis can
restore the amino group.
The usual acetanilide comparison favours a para nitro derivative while
allowing
an ortho product.
Do not confuse adding a nitro group to the ring with oxidizing the existing
amino nitrogen into a nitro substituent.
Draw the protonated or protected starting species before assigning electron
donation, orientation and the final workup product.
An amino substituent activates an aromatic ring in some reactions, but that
does not guarantee compatibility with every electrophilic substitution
reagent.
In the usual aluminium chloride mediated Friedel Crafts comparison, aniline's
nitrogen acts as a Lewis base and binds the Lewis acid.
The lone pair used in coordination is no longer available in the same way to
activate the ring, and the resulting strongly deactivating complex prevents
the
ordinary clean ring alkylation prediction.
Therefore benzene and aniline cannot simply be assigned the same alkyl
chloride
and aluminium chloride arrow with only a change in directing position.
This limitation concerns that reagent system, not universal chemical inertness
of aniline.
Also distinguish ring acylation from nitrogen acylation: formation of
acetanilide makes a new nitrogen carbonyl bond and is not proof that a Friedel
Crafts carbon carbon bond formed on the ring.
When a question proposes aniline becoming an ethyl substituted aniline through
the usual Friedel Crafts conditions, flag the incompatibility before counting
ortho and para products.
Check Lewis acid binding, substrate activation and the atom actually receiving
a new group as three separate decisions.
A diazonium replacement must name the incoming group and the appropriate
reaction route.
In the classical Balz Schiemann map, an arenediazonium tetrafluoroborate gives
an aryl fluoride with nitrogen gas and boron trifluoride on decomposition
under
the specified reaction conditions.
For a benzene derived example, the organic product is fluorobenzene, with the
six ring carbons retained.
The net atom ledger starts with four fluorines in tetrafluoroborate: one
enters
the aryl fluoride and three remain with boron in boron trifluoride.
Both nitrogens of the diazonium group leave together as one nitrogen molecule.
This differs from the familiar copper one chloride or bromide replacement
maps;
drawing copper fluoride as though all copper assisted replacement reagents
were
interchangeable is not the intended classical route.
Replacing the amino derived diazonium group by fluorine adds no carbon and
leaves no nitrogen in the selected organic product.
The reaction name describes a controlled chemical transformation, not a
guarantee that every substituted ring behaves identically.
This chapter supplies reaction and atom accounting, not instructions for
isolating or heating a diazonium salt.
Keep the counterion, organic substitution and gaseous products distinct.
An amino group can help choose where another group enters an aromatic ring and
then be removed from the final framework.
In the familiar deamination map, a primary aromatic amine is first converted
to
an arenediazonium species.
Reduction with hypophosphorous acid replaces the diazonium group by hydrogen
while nitrogen gas is released.
Consider a ring labelled with amino at carbon one, methyl at carbon four, and
bromines already at carbons two and six.
Those bromines are ortho to the amino group in the supplied precursor.
Replacing the amino derived diazonium group by hydrogen preserves the ring and
methyl carbons.
Renumbering the product from its methyl substituent places the bromines at
positions three and five, giving three five dibromotoluene.
The bromine atoms have not migrated; only the naming reference changed after
the directing group was removed.
This can achieve a substitution pattern that direct bromination of toluene
would not normally favour.
The example starts from the specified substituted precursor and does not
assume
an unqualified bromination gives a single pure product.
Follow the original ring labels through replacement before assigning the final
product name.
The class of an amine product depends on which groups remain attached to
nitrogen, not just on whether a carbonyl was reduced.
Use a specified reductive amination map starting from acetaldehyde and
methylamine.
Condensation gives an imine intermediate, meaning a carbon nitrogen double
bond
compound, with an ethylidene carbon nitrogen double bond and the original
methyl group still bonded to nitrogen.
The carbonyl oxygen leaves in the water balance rather than remaining in the
selected carbon nitrogen double bond intermediate.
Reducing the carbon nitrogen double bond then gives ethylmethylamine.
Nitrogen is bonded to an ethyl group, a methyl group and one hydrogen, so the
product is a secondary amine.
The organic inventory is three carbons: two from acetaldehyde and one from
methylamine.
In formal atom bookkeeping, acetaldehyde plus methylamine plus two reducing
hydrogen equivalents gives the three carbon amine plus water.
Direct reduction of acetaldehyde alone would instead give ethanol, a different
functional group.
Actual reductive amination requires suitable control of condensation and
reduction, and competing reactions can affect yield.
This supporting reaction map identifies connectivity and atom sources rather
than prescribing a complete reagent sequence or claiming exclusive conversion.
Partition of an amine requires both its acid base equilibrium and its neutral
species partition coefficient.
In a supplied supporting model, neutral base B distributes between an organic
phase and water with coefficient P equal to twenty, defined as organic neutral
concentration divided by aqueous neutral concentration.
Protonated base remains in water.
The conjugate acid has supplied p K a ten, and an external buffer maintains
the
stated aqueous p H.
The ratio of protonated to neutral base in water is ten raised to p K a minus
p
H.
The total organic to aqueous analytical distribution ratio is consequently P
divided by one plus that ratio.
At p H eight, D is twenty over one hundred one.
For one hundred millilitres water and fifty millilitres organic phase, the
fraction of total amine in organic solution is ten over one hundred eleven,
about nine point zero one percent.
At p H ten, D becomes ten and the organic fraction five sixths, about eighty
three point three percent.
These results assume equilibrium, unchanged phase volumes, no ion transfer
into
organic solution and no additional association.
The supplied p H is maintained rather than calculated from the amine alone.
A diazonium ion can act as an electrophile toward a sufficiently activated
aromatic ring.
In a selected coupling with phenol, the new bond joins a carbon of the phenol
ring to the terminal nitrogen of the diazonium group.
The product contains an azo bridge between two aromatic systems; it is not
made
by simply joining the two oxygen atoms or removing both nitrogen atoms.
If the para position of phenol is available, para coupling is commonly
favoured
in the elementary map, while a blocked position changes the available sites.
Solution conditions matter because phenoxide is a stronger ring activator than
neutral phenol.
For an arylamine coupling component, excessive protonation of the amino group
instead reduces its ability to activate the ring.
These observations do not justify choosing an arbitrarily extreme pH: the
diazonium partner also has condition dependent stability and competing
reactions.
Treat the stated medium as part of the reaction identity.
Colour is consistent with an extended conjugated product, but colour alone
does
not establish the complete connectivity or purity of an unknown dye.
Two transformations of the same primary amide can produce amines with
different
carbon skeletons.
Take benzamide, with a benzene ring directly attached to a carbonyl carbon and
that carbonyl attached to an amino group.
Suitable amide reduction converts the carbonyl carbon into a methylene without
deleting it.
The product is benzylamine, in which nitrogen is bonded to a saturated carbon
outside the ring.
In a Hofmann rearrangement of a primary amide, the carbonyl carbon is removed
from the organic amine skeleton.
Benzamide therefore gives aniline instead, with nitrogen directly attached to
the aromatic ring.
Both products are primary amines because nitrogen has one carbon substituent,
but only aniline is an arylamine in this comparison.
Apply the same bookkeeping to phenylacetamide, which already has a methylene
between ring and carbonyl: its Hofmann product is benzylamine, not aniline.
Count and mark the carbonyl carbon before choosing the product name.
Reagent compatibility and actual yield remain separate questions, and Hofmann

In a selected dry salt calculation, a pure monobasic amine sample has amount
twenty millimoles and mass one point four six grams.
Complete formation of its anhydrous hydrochloride increases the mass by twenty
millimoles times thirty six point five grams per mole, or zero point seven
three grams.
The ideal salt mass is therefore two point one nine grams, and the starting
amine molar mass is seventy three grams per mole.
These numbers do not distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary structural
isomers with that molar mass.
